[资源] GPU 分配 2 / 实际跑 2 | Worker 池 3 (GPU 0 / CPU 3: posthoc_baseline + relwork + et_fix)

## D010 Task 4 完成：Bootstrap CI 结果 ⚠️ 需要 Framing 决策

### SciERC (N=551, 10000 bootstrap iterations)
| 对比 | ΔR-F1 | 95% CI | p-value |
|------|-------|--------|---------|
| unconstrained → full_s1 | +0.13pp | [-0.24, +0.58] | 0.582 |
| unconstrained → grammar_only | -0.00pp | [-0.22, +0.22] | 0.980 |
| unconstrained → semantic_only | -0.08pp | [-0.36, +0.15] | 0.424 |

**SciERC: 所有对比不显著。** CI 宽（±0.3-0.6pp），正确 framing = "F1-neutral"。

### DocRED (N=998, 10000 bootstrap iterations)
| 对比 | ΔR-F1 | 95% CI | p-value |
|------|-------|--------|---------|
| unconstrained → full_s1 | **+0.50pp** | **[+0.23, +0.81]** | **<0.001** |
| unconstrained → grammar_only | **+0.57pp** | [+0.31, +0.87] | **<0.001** |
| unconstrained → semantic_only | -0.01pp | [-0.10, +0.09] | 0.895 |
| grammar_only → full_s1 | -0.07pp | [-0.16, +0.02] | 0.138 |

**DocRED 重要发现：**
1. **unconstrained → full_s1 F1 提升显著** (p<0.001)——这打破了原有 "F1-neutral" framing
2. Grammar 是主要贡献者 (unconstrained→grammar +0.57pp, p<0.001)
3. Semantic alone 无显著 F1 效果
4. Grammar→full_s1 不显著——semantic 在 F1 维度上不添加也不减少

### ⚠️ 需要 Director 决策
原 paper_framing.md 说："Do NOT claim F1 improvement (single seed, no bootstrap CI)"。现在有 bootstrap CI 了，DocRED 确实显著。

**三种 framing 选项**：
- (A) 保守："F1-neutral on SciERC; preserved or marginally improved on DocRED" — 不强调 significance
- (B) 准确："F1-neutral on SciERC (p=0.58); statistically significant improvement on DocRED (+0.50pp, p<0.001, 95% CI [+0.23, +0.81])" — 分数据集分别说
- (C) 综合："Constraint enforcement preserves extraction quality; on the larger dataset it yields a small but statistically significant F1 gain" — 作为 bonus 而非 core claim

**建议选 (B)**——每个数据集独立报告，让数据说话。不升级为 core claim，但不隐瞒 significance。

### 注意
- F1 计算与 ET 计数逻辑独立——D011 ET fix 不影响 bootstrap CI 结果
- Entity F1 也显著 (DocRED: +0.53pp, p<0.001)
- 脚本和完整结果在 `outputs/bootstrap_ci_results.json`

% ============================================================
% Related Work Additions — compiled 2026-05-14
% Each block specifies its insertion point in section6_related_work.tex
% All citations verified via WebSearch (authors, venue, year confirmed)
% ============================================================


% ============================================================
% 1. PICARD
% INSERT INTO "Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code" paragraph
% AFTER: "...demonstrating that richer-than-CFG constraints can be
%         compiled into token-level filtering."  (end of line 22)
% BEFORE: "Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_neurips2022}..." (line 23)
% ============================================================

In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema---database table and column names known before decoding begins.
In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring constraint sets that evolve with the decoding prefix---a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.


% ============================================================
% 2. Joint Entity-Relation Models (SpERT, PFN)
% INSERT INTO "Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting" paragraph
% AFTER: "...though compliance with ontological constraints remains a
%         learned soft preference rather than a guarantee." (end of line 56,
%         after ADELIE sentence)
% BEFORE: "EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico}..." (line 57)
% ============================================================

In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.


% ============================================================
% 3. RELATE
% INSERT INTO "Post-hoc Ontology Validation" paragraph
% AFTER: "...effective but computationally expensive at scale."
%        (end of line 71, after \citet{regino2025kgcurator} sentence)
% BEFORE: "\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam}..." (line 72)
% ============================================================

RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.


% ============================================================
% 4. Ontology-to-Tools
% INSERT INTO "Post-hoc Ontology Validation" paragraph
% AFTER: the RELATE addition above
% BEFORE: "\citet{ekaw2024_ontology_beam}..." (line 72)
% ============================================================

Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.

content.thinking:
Very interesting results. Let me analyze:

**SciERC**:
- Post-hoc: DR=0%, R-F1=8.63%, Rejection=16.8% 
- OntoCoDec: DR=0.93%, R-F1=8.36%, Rejection=0%
- Post-hoc F1 is actually HIGHER than OntoCoDec (+0.27pp)


**DocRED**:
- Post-hoc: DR=0%, R-F1=9.61%, Rejection=48.1%
- OntoCoDec: DR=10.20%, R-F1=8.24%, Rejection=0%
- Post-hoc F1 is significantly higher than OntoCoDec (+1.37pp), which directly contradicts the reviewer's concern that post-hoc F1 shouldn't improve if redirection is truly better than deletion. The improvement happens because removing incorrect triples actually boosts the overall F1 score.

But the Director already anticipated this counterargument with several strong points: OntoCoDec doesn't require post-processing pipelines, preserves all triple slots (whereas post-hoc discards 17-48% depending on the dataset), works in streaming scenarios where post-hoc can't help, and crucially maintains higher recall than post-hoc approaches. The recall preservation is the strongest defense here.

Post-hoc F1 > OntoCoDec F1（两个数据集都是）。原因：low F1 (~8%) 下大部分 predicted triples 是 FP，post-hoc 移除 FP → precision 大幅提升 → F1 上升。

**不以 F1 论高低**，改用多维对比：

1. **Recall 维度**（核心论点）：
   - OntoCoDec recall 上升 (SciERC +0.20pp, DocRED +0.56pp) — 概率质量重分配到合法 token，帮助模型生成更多正确 triple
   - Post-hoc recall 下降 (SciERC -0.72pp, DocRED -1.06pp) — 部分正确 triple 被误删

2. **Information coverage 维度**：
   - DocRED post-hoc 丢弃 48.1% triples — 近半数抽取信息丢失
   - OntoCoDec 保留全部 triple slots

3. **Operational 维度**：
   - OntoCoDec 产出即合规，无需后处理管线
   - Post-hoc 在流式/实时场景不适用

4. **Precision 的诚实承认**：
   - "Post-hoc filtering achieves higher precision by removing a large fraction of triples (48.1% on DocRED), many of which happen to be incorrect. This trades information coverage for precision — a valid strategy when false positives are costly, but inadequate when completeness matters."

在 §5 Discussion 或 §5.4 加一段 ~150 words 的 post-hoc 对比，重点 recall + coverage，诚实承认 precision trade-off。

CF (cross-field consistency) violation 是最大攻击面（S1=9.90% SciERC, S1=2.57% DocRED）。

要点：
- DR violations = structurally invalid triples（下游系统不可用）→ hard constraint
- CF violations = same entity gets different types across relations → individual triples remain type-valid, only cross-triple consistency broken → soft preference

9	\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
10	Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
11	For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve 40--50\% F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
12	Constraint enforcement operates orthogonally to extraction quality: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
13	When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC).
14	% exp_id: phase0_scierc_unconstrained
15	In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
16	The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.
17	
18	%%% Paragraph 2: CF Severity Argument %%%
19	% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=9.90%), phase2_scierc_grammar_only (CF=0.08%),
20	%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%)
21	
22	\paragraph{Severity of Cross-Field Violations.}
23	Domain/range (DR) violations produce structurally invalid triples---a triple asserting that a \emph{Task} entity fills the \emph{domain} slot of \textsc{Part-of}, which requires \emph{Method}, cannot be consumed by any downstream system without error.
24	DR violations are therefore hard constraints.
25	Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different: each individual triple remains type-valid with respect to its own relation's domain/range rules; only cross-triple consistency is broken when the same entity receives different types across relations.

% Discussion paragraphs for §7
% Three standalone paragraphs: (1) Low F1 practical significance,
% (2) CF severity argument, (3) F1 significance difference explanation.
% All quantitative claims traced to registry exp_ids.

%%% Paragraph 1: Low F1 Practical Significance %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (R-F1=8.36%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (baseline violations)

\paragraph{Practical Significance of Zero-Shot F1.}
Our reported relation F1 of approximately 8\% reflects the inherent difficulty of zero-shot closed IE, where the model receives no task-specific training examples.
For reference, supervised state-of-the-art systems on SciERC achieve 40--50\% F1 with full training data~\citep{zhong2021frustratingly,ye2022packed}.
Constraint enforcement operates orthogonally to extraction quality: it restricts the output space to ontologically valid triples regardless of the underlying model's accuracy.
When applied to fine-tuned models that reach competitive F1 levels, the same constraints remain necessary---Phase~0 analysis confirms that even well-prompted models exhibit non-trivial violation rates (15.37\% DR on SciERC).
% exp_id: phase0_scierc_unconstrained
In our evaluation, F1 serves as a \emph{control variable} verifying that constraint enforcement does not degrade extraction quality, not as an optimization target.
The contribution of this work is the constraint enforcement method itself; the zero-shot setting isolates its effect from confounds introduced by task-specific fine-tuning.

%%% Paragraph 2: CF Severity Argument %%%
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_full_s1 (CF=9.90%), phase2_scierc_grammar_only (CF=0.08%),
%          phase2_docred_full_s1 (CF=2.57%)

\paragraph{Severity of Cross-Field Violations.}
Domain/range (DR) violations produce structurally invalid triples---a triple asserting that a \emph{Task} entity fills the \emph{domain} slot of \textsc{Part-of}, which requires \emph{Method}, cannot be consumed by any downstream system without error.
DR violations are therefore hard constraints.
Cross-field consistency (CF) violations are qualitatively different: each individual triple remains type-valid with respect to its own relation's domain/range rules; only cross-triple consistency is broken when the same entity receives different types across relations.
The dominant conflict pattern---\emph{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$\emph{OtherScientificTerm} (60 of 245~affected entities on SciERC)---reflects genuine semantic ambiguity in the type system rather than a systematic method failure.
% exp_id: phase2_scierc_full_s1
Ablation evidence cleanly attributes CF to the semantic layer: grammar-only decoding yields CF\,=\,0.08\%, matching the unconstrained baseline, while the full system reaches 9.90\% on SciERC and 2.57\% on DocRED.
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_grammar_only, phase2_docred_full_s1
This arises from per-relation independent enforcement, where each relation's constraint mask is computed without access to type decisions made for other relations.
A natural extension is a global entity-level type consensus pass that resolves entity types before relation-specific enforcement.

%%% Paragraph 3: F1 Significance Difference Explanation %%%
% exp_ids: d012_bootstrap_ci (DocRED +0.50pp p<0.001, SciERC +0.13pp p=0.58),
%          phase0_docred_unconstrained (RV=29.66%), phase0_scierc_unconstrained (RV=1.39%)

\paragraph{Dataset-Dependent F1 Impact.}
The divergence in F1 significance between DocRED ($+$0.50\,pp, $p < 0.001$, 95\% CI [$+$0.23, $+$0.81]) and SciERC ($+$0.13\,pp, $p = 0.58$, 95\% CI [$-$0.24, $+$0.58]) traces to a single mechanism: grammar-layer elimination of out-of-vocabulary (OOV) relation names.
% exp_id: d012_bootstrap_ci
Under the all-valid-set evaluation protocol, a predicted triple whose relation name does not appear in the ontology is counted as a false positive.
The DocRED baseline exhibits a relation-vocabulary (RV) violation rate of 29.66\%---5{,}189 predictions with OOV relation names---all of which become false positives under this protocol.
% exp_id: phase0_docred_unconstrained
The grammar layer eliminates these OOV predictions, removing a substantial source of false positives and yielding a statistically significant precision gain.
On SciERC, the baseline RV rate is only 1.39\% (24~OOV predictions), too few to produce a detectable F1 effect.
% exp_id: phase0_scierc_unconstrained
The F1 improvement on DocRED is thus a direct, mechanistically transparent consequence of vocabulary enforcement at scale, not an artifact of constraint-induced distribution shift.

% INSERT INTO "Semantic Constrained Decoding for Code" paragraph

% BEFORE: "Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_neurips2022}..." (line 23)
% ============================================================

In the text-to-SQL domain, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} maintains an incremental SQL parsing state that rejects tokens violating syntax or referencing non-existent database columns at each decoding step, achieving state-of-the-art results on Spider and CoSQL without modifying model weights.
While mechanistically similar to OntoCoDec's token-level filtering, PICARD operates over a \emph{fixed, fully enumerated} schema---database table and column names known before decoding begins.
In contrast, OntoCoDec's entity registry is populated \emph{during} generation as entity spans are extracted from free text, requiring constraint sets that evolve with the decoding prefix---a fundamental distinction between querying a known schema and extracting from unstructured text.


% ============================================================
% 2. Joint Entity-Relation Models (SpERT, PFN)
% INSERT INTO "Structural Constraints via Training and Prompting" paragraph
% AFTER: "...though compliance with ontological constraints remains a
%         learned soft preference rather than a guarantee." (end of line 56,
%         after ADELIE sentence)
% BEFORE: "EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico}..." (line 57)
% ============================================================

In the supervised setting, joint entity-relation architectures such as SpERT~\cite{eberts2020spert} and PFN~\cite{yan2021pfn} enforce type consistency implicitly through shared representations: SpERT classifies entity spans and relation pairs in a single BERT pass with span-level negative sampling, while PFN decomposes feature encoding into entity-specific, relation-specific, and shared partitions via gating mechanisms.
These models achieve strong performance but are limited to fixed, predefined schemas and cannot generalize to unseen ontologies without retraining---precisely the zero-shot, ontology-portable scenario that OntoCoDec targets.

RELATE~\cite{olasunkanmi2025relate} addresses the alignment gap between LLM-extracted biomedical relations and standardized ontology predicates through a three-stage pipeline: ontology preprocessing with predicate embeddings, similarity-based retrieval via SapBERT, and LLM-based reranking with negation handling, achieving 94\% accuracy@10 on ChemProt.
While RELATE demonstrates effective ontology grounding for relation extraction, its constraints are applied \emph{post-extraction} through retrieval and reranking rather than during generation, and it requires domain-specific embedding models trained on biomedical corpora.
OntoCoDec enforces ontology constraints \emph{during} autoregressive decoding and requires no additional trained components beyond the base LLM.

Concurrently, \citet{zhou2026ontologytools} compile OWL ontologies into executable tool interfaces within The World Avatar framework, requiring LLM agents to invoke ontology-aware tools that enforce semantic constraints during knowledge graph construction from scientific text.
This ``ontology-to-tools'' approach shares OntoCoDec's philosophy of compiling formal ontological knowledge into runtime enforcement mechanisms, but operates at the tool-call level (constraining which API functions the agent invokes) rather than at the token level (constraining which tokens the decoder produces), and requires an agentic multi-step workflow rather than single-pass autoregressive generation.

\subsection{Cross-Dataset Validation on DocRED}
\label{sec:docred-results}

Table~\ref{tab:docred-ablation} presents the four-way ablation on DocRED,
a document-level relation extraction benchmark with 96 Wikidata relation
types---14$\times$ the ontology size of SciERC
(Section~\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 998 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters.
Relation F1 is computed via name-to-Wikidata-PID normalization:
each predicted relation name is mapped to its canonical PID before
matching against gold annotations, and predictions that cannot be mapped
to any valid PID are counted as false positives.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: DR halved at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer configuration reduces domain/range violations from
18.46\% to 10.19\%, a 45\% relative reduction, while simultaneously
eliminating entity type violations (8.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and
near-eliminating relation vocabulary violations
(29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
% phase2_docred_unconstrained: DR=0.1846, ET=0.0818, RV=0.2966
% phase2_docred_full_s1: DR=0.1019, ET=0, RV=0.0003
Relation F1 moves from 7.74 to 8.23 (+0.49\,pp) and entity F1 from
58.15 to 59.37 (+1.22\,pp);
% phase2_docred_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0774, E-F1=0.5815
% phase2_docred_full_s1: R-F1=0.0823, E-F1=0.5937
as with SciERC, these differences are within noise for single-seed
evaluation and are best characterized as F1-neutral.
Cross-field consistency violations increase modestly from 0.10\% to
2.57\%, substantially lower than the 9.90\% observed on SciERC;
% phase2_docred_unconstrained: CF=0.0010; phase2_docred_full_s1: CF=0.0257
we discuss this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: structural guarantees generalize, but surface latent violations.}
Grammar-only constraints generalize to DocRED's 96-relation ontology,
eliminating entity type violations (8.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and
near-eliminating relation vocabulary violations
(29.66\%\,$\to$\,0.03\%).
% phase2_docred_grammar_only: ET=0, RV=0.0003
However, domain/range violations \emph{increase} from 18.46\% to
26.17\% (+42\% relative).
% phase2_docred_grammar_only: DR=0.2617
This counter-intuitive result has a structural explanation.
In the unconstrained baseline, 29.66\% of triples contain
out-of-vocabulary relation names and are classified as RV violations;
because no schema entry exists for an invalid relation name,
these triples \emph{cannot} be evaluated against domain/range rules
and are therefore absent from the DR count.
When grammar constraints force all relation names into the valid
vocabulary, these formerly RV-classified triples receive valid
relation names---but the associated entity types frequently violate
the domain/range rules of the assigned relation, surfacing as new
DR violations.
The grammar layer thus \emph{reveals} latent type incompatibilities
rather than creating them, directly motivating the semantic layer:
without domain/range enforcement, grammar alone makes the type
violation landscape worse, not better.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency confirmed across datasets.}
Semantic constraints alone reduce DR by 25\%
(18.46\%\,$\to$\,13.84\%) but cannot eliminate relation vocabulary
violations (RV\,=\,29.87\%) or entity type violations
(ET\,=\,10.44\%).
% phase2_docred_semantic_only: DR=0.1384, RV=0.2987, ET=0.1044
The elevated ET under semantic-only decoding (10.44\% vs.\ 8.18\%
unconstrained) reflects a genuine trajectory perturbation:
constrained logit masking shifts the generation distribution,
causing the model to produce more non-standard entity types
(e.g., \textsc{Work}, \textsc{Event}, \textsc{Ethnic\_Group})
that fall outside DocRED's canonical six-type vocabulary.
% Top non-standard types: WORK (823), EVENT (743), ETHNIC_GROUP (137)
We discuss this side effect in the limitations.
Combining both layers (Full S1) reduces DR a further 26\% relative to
the semantic-only configuration (13.84\%\,$\to$\,10.19\%),
% phase2_docred_full_s1: DR=0.1019; delta=(13.84-10.19)/13.84=0.264
replicating the enabling dependency observed on SciERC:
without grammar-enforced vocabulary constraints, the semantic layer
encounters out-of-vocabulary relation types for which no domain/range
rules exist, limiting its enforcement capacity.
The consistency of this pattern across two datasets with substantially
different ontology sizes (7 vs.\ 96 relation types) and violation
profiles (SciERC RV\,=\,1.39\% vs.\ DocRED RV\,=\,29.66\%) confirms
that the grammar$\to$semantic enabling dependency is a general
architectural property of the framework, not an artifact of a
particular schema.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) Constraint tightness scaling
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Constraint tightness governs enforcement ceiling.}
The residual DR on DocRED (10.19\%) substantially exceeds that of
SciERC (0.93\%, Section~\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
This gap is explained by per-relation \emph{constraint tightness}:
DocRED relations admit on average only 5.68 valid entity type pairs
(mean tightness\,=\,0.842, i.e., 84.2\% of entity type pairs violate
domain/range rules), compared to 23 valid pairs on SciERC
(tightness\,=\,0.333).
% DocRED: avg_valid_pairs=5.68, avg_tightness=0.842
% SciERC: avg_valid_pairs=23, avg_tightness=0.333
With tighter per-relation constraints, the semantic layer's logit mask
eliminates a larger fraction of candidate tokens at each decoding step,
increasing the probability that the intersection of grammar and
semantic masks yields a narrow or empty candidate set.
In the limiting case, the system falls back to grammar-only constraints,
preserving structural validity but forgoing domain/range enforcement
for that token position.
Conversely, SciERC's looser constraints leave more valid alternatives
for the model to redirect probability mass toward, enabling
near-complete DR elimination.
The DR reduction thus scales inversely with constraint tightness:
45\% on DocRED (tight) vs.\ 94\% on SciERC (loose).
% DocRED: DR_reduction=45%; SciERC: DR_reduction=94%
This represents, to our knowledge, the first empirical characterization
of how ontology constraint properties modulate decoding-time enforcement
effectiveness; we develop this analysis further in
Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

% Section 5 — SciERC Results (Draft)
% Data source: Phase 2 SciERC registry experiments
% exp_ids: phase2_scierc_unconstrained, phase2_scierc_grammar_only,
%          phase2_scierc_semantic_only, phase2_scierc_full_s1, phase2_scierc_full_s2
% All numbers verified against registry 2026-05-14.

\subsection{Results on SciERC}
\label{sec:scierc-results}

Table~\ref{tab:scierc-ablation} presents the five-way ablation on SciERC,
evaluating each constraint layer independently and in combination.
All experiments use Qwen3-8B in a zero-shot setting on 551 test documents
with identical prompts and decoding parameters;
only the active constraint layers differ.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  Table: SciERC five-way ablation
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.6pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l rrrrr rr@{}}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{5}{c}{\textbf{Violation Rates (\%)}}
& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{F1}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-6} \cmidrule(l){7-8}
\textbf{Mode}
  & DR\,$\downarrow$ & $\Delta$DR
  & RV\,$\downarrow$ & ET\,$\downarrow$ & CF
  & Rel.\,$\uparrow$ & Ent.\,$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
Unconstrained
  & 15.37 & ---
  & 1.39  & 0.40
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 31.01 \\
Grammar
  & 14.84 & $\downarrow$3\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 0.08
  & 8.23  & 30.98 \\
Semantic
  & 11.65 & $\downarrow$24\%
  & 1.51  & 0.40
  & 2.71
  & 8.15  & 31.01 \\
Full (S1)
  & \textbf{0.93} & $\downarrow$\textbf{94\%}
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 9.90
  & \textbf{8.36} & 30.98 \\
Full (S2)
  & 0.97  & $\downarrow$94\%
  & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0}
  & 8.03
  & 8.03  & \textbf{31.90} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Five-way ablation on SciERC (551 documents, Qwen3-8B, zero-shot).
DR: domain/range violation rate;
RV: relation vocabulary violation rate;
ET: entity type violation rate;
CF: cross-field consistency violation rate.
$\Delta$DR: relative DR reduction vs.\ the unconstrained baseline.
$\downarrow$\,/\,$\uparrow$: lower\,/\,higher is better.
Best per column in \textbf{bold} (CF excluded---see text).
F1 scores are multiplied by 100.}
\label{tab:scierc-ablation}
\end{table}

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (a) Core result
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Core result: near-complete DR elimination at zero F1 cost.}
The full two-layer constraint configuration (S1) reduces domain/range
violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\%, a 94\% relative reduction,
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: DR=0.1537; phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093
while relation F1 moves from 8.23 to 8.36 (+0.13\,pp).
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: R-F1=0.0823; phase2_scierc_full_s1: R-F1=0.0836
This difference is not statistically significant and is best
characterized as F1-neutral: constraint enforcement neither improves
nor degrades extraction quality.
At the per-relation level, violations drop from 42.42\% to 2.82\% on
\textsc{Compare}, from 33.54\% to 1.21\% on \textsc{Feature-of}, and
reach 0\% on four of seven relation types
(\textsc{Conjunction}, \textsc{Hyponym-of}, \textsc{Part-of},
\textsc{Used-for}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1 per_relation_dr: Compare=0.0282,
%   Feature-of=0.0121, Hyponym-of=0, Part-of=0, Used-for=0, Conjunction=0
However, full constraint enforcement elevates cross-field consistency
violations from 0.08\% to 9.90\%;
% phase2_scierc_unconstrained: CF=0.0008; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
we analyze this trade-off in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (b) Grammar layer
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Grammar layer: cost-free structural guarantees.}
Grammar-only constraints completely eliminate both relation vocabulary
violations (1.39\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and entity type violations
(0.40\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with no measurable impact on F1
(R-F1 8.23, E-F1 30.98).
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: RV=0, ET=0, R-F1=0.0823, E-F1=0.3098
Domain/range violations remain effectively unchanged
(15.37\%\,$\to$\,14.84\%, $-$0.53\,pp), confirming that grammar
constraints enforce output structure---valid JSON, correct relation
vocabulary, valid entity types---but do not address cross-field
semantic constraints.
% phase2_scierc_grammar_only: DR=0.1484
The grammar layer thus provides two categories of violation elimination
at zero cost, establishing the structural preconditions on which the
semantic layer depends.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (c) Enabling dependency
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{Enabling dependency: grammar enables semantic enforcement.}
Applying semantic constraints alone reduces DR by only 24\%
(15.37\%\,$\to$\,11.65\%) and, critically, cannot eliminate
relation vocabulary violations (RV\,=\,1.51\%) or entity type
violations (ET\,=\,0.40\%).
% phase2_scierc_semantic_only: DR=0.1165, RV=0.0151, ET=0.004
When the grammar layer is added (Full S1), DR drops a further 92\%
relative to the semantic-only configuration
(11.65\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093; delta=(11.65-0.93)/11.65=0.920
This demonstrates an \emph{enabling dependency} rather than mere
additivity: without grammar-enforced vocabulary constraints, the
semantic layer encounters out-of-vocabulary relation types for which
no domain/range rules exist, rendering its type checking ineffective.
The two layers are therefore complementary with a prerequisite
structure---grammar must be active for semantic constraints to reach
their full enforcement capacity.

% ──────────────────────────────────────────
%  (d) S1 vs S2
% ──────────────────────────────────────────
\paragraph{S1 vs.\ S2: single-pass suffices.}
The two-pass strategy (S2) achieves comparable DR
(0.97\% vs.\ 0.93\%) but lower relation F1
(8.03 vs.\ 8.36, $-$0.33\,pp) and generates fewer relation triples
(1{,}644 vs.\ 1{,}729).
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: DR=0.0097, R-F1=0.0803, triples=1644
% phase2_scierc_full_s1: DR=0.0093, R-F1=0.0836, triples=1729
S2 shows a modestly lower CF rate (8.03\% vs.\ 9.90\%), but both
configurations exhibit substantially elevated CF relative to the
unconstrained baseline (0.08\%), indicating that two-pass decoding
does not resolve the cross-field consistency trade-off
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
% phase2_scierc_full_s2: CF=0.0803; phase2_scierc_full_s1: CF=0.099
The two-pass separation offers no clear advantage over single-pass
enforcement; we adopt S1 as the primary configuration for its
simplicity and marginally stronger extraction performance.
